title: Ragtime
objective: After this level you can describe ragtime and Scott Joplin.
summary: Ragtime set a syncopated right hand over a steady left-hand beat. Scott Joplin, the King of Ragtime, wrote "Maple Leaf Rag" (1899) and won a posthumous Pulitzer.

cards.headline: Ragtime piano sounds like two hands arguing about where the beat is.
cards.body: Put on a rag and your foot finds the beat at once. Then the melody jumps in just off it, again and again. That friendly tug-of-war made ragtime the leading style of American popular music from about 1899 to 1917. Here's how it works, and who did it best.

cards.headline: The left hand keeps time; the right hand plays with it
cards.body: Remember Level 4's beat, the steady pulse you tap your foot to? In ragtime piano, the left hand guards it with regularly accented bass notes and chords. Over the top, the right hand plays a bouncing melody that keeps accenting notes off the beat. That's syncopation, and to "rag" a tune simply meant to syncopate its melody. The style drew on African American banjo playing and the syncopated dance rhythms of the cakewalk.

cards.headline: Scott Joplin, the King of Ragtime
cards.body: Scott Joplin, an African American composer born in Texas in 1867 or 1868, became known as the King of Ragtime. His "Maple Leaf Rag," published in 1899, was the most successful of the early rags and became the style's signature piece. Joplin aimed high: he wrote a three-act opera, Treemonisha, and published it at his own expense in 1911.

cards.fact: Scott Joplin won a Pulitzer Prize in 1976, decades after he died.
cards.context: Joplin died in 1917. In the 1970s his music came roaring back in the Oscar-winning score of the film The Sting, and in 1976 the Pulitzer board gave him a special award for his contributions to American music. Ragtime itself was one forerunner of jazz, which is where this chapter heads next.

mascot.line: That is a very long wait for applause. The music was patient.
